prompt:
Some people say that the best way to improve public health is by increasing the number of
sports facilities. Others, however, say that this would have little effect on public health and that other measures are required.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
intro_note: Written after panel convergence. A practice rewrite targeting Band 7, not an independently graded script. Keeps your position and distance argument; adds a developed nutrition alternative. Examples are hypothetical.

spans.text: Some people regard building more sports facilities as the best way to improve public health, while others believe that different measures are needed.
Although nearby facilities can encourage regular exercise

highlight.label: Controlled concession
highlight.explanation: Concedes the access benefit before stating your reservation; this is a structure you already attempt.

spans.text: , I believe they are
insufficient on their own

highlight.label: Keep the claim proportional
highlight.explanation: Preserves your position without claiming that facilities have negligible benefits for the whole population.

spans.text: because people's health also depends on their everyday habits,
including diet

highlight.label: Preview the alternative
highlight.explanation: Introduces the alternative developed in the second body.

spans.text: Supporters of additional facilities argue that
convenient access

highlight.label: Use access as a noun
highlight.explanation: Access is a noun here. Compare: residents can access a pool; residents have access to a pool.

spans.text: makes it easier to stay active. When the nearest swimming pool or sports centre requires a long journey, residents may struggle to fit exercise around work and family responsibilities.
Consider a resident in Korea

highlight.label: Hypothetical example
highlight.explanation: Makes your distance argument concrete without presenting an invented national trend as fact.

spans.text: who has stopped swimming because the nearest pool is too far from home.
If a new pool opened nearby, this person might return regularly

highlight.label: Second conditional
highlight.explanation: If + past form, then might + base verb describes a hypothetical change and its possible result.

spans.text: gradually improving their fitness

highlight.label: Complete the health link
highlight.explanation: Participation leads to an explicit health benefit, completing the argument for facilities.

spans.text: . By reducing the time and effort needed to participate, local facilities can help people
maintain an exercise routine

highlight.label: Learn the whole combination
highlight.explanation: A precise, reusable alternative to start or continue their sports activity.

spans.text: . This gives supporters a practical reason to prioritise investment in them.
However, easier access may have little effect on people who are not interested in sport

highlight.label: One transition
highlight.explanation: Places the objection at the start of the alternative argument, avoiding its repetition across both bodies.

spans.text: , and it does not address unhealthy eating habits. Other measures are therefore needed to improve health more widely. Schools could provide

highlight.explanation: Names a concrete policy and explains what learners could change.

spans.text: Offering healthier lunches would support these lessons

highlight.label: Gerund subject and reference
highlight.explanation: Offering healthier lunches acts as the subject; these lessons points back to nutrition lessons.

spans.text: by making nutritious food available during the school day. Such measures could improve pupils' diets
regardless of whether they enjoy competitive sports

highlight.explanation: Connects dietary measures to your original concern about people with little interest in sport.

spans.text: . In my view, combining education with practical support offers a stronger response than relying on additional buildings alone.
In conclusion, more local sports facilities can
remove a barrier to regular exercise

highlight.explanation: States what facilities can do without claiming that access solves every problem.

spans.text: and improve fitness. Nevertheless, I believe they should form part of
